highlights.title: The AI Layoff Trap: Automation Arms Race Erodes Consumer Demand
highlights.summary: Falk and Tsoukalas model a competitive 'automation arms race' in which rational firms displace workers faster than the economy can reabsorb them, creating a demand externality that ultimately harms the firms themselves. The paper shows that awareness of this trap is insufficient to stop it under competitive market conditions, implying structural policy intervention may be required. This is one of the most directly relevant pieces to aggregate displacement dynamics published in the lookback window.

highlights.title: Labor Theory of Value Revisited: AI and Digital Platforms Challenge Classical Wage Models
highlights.summary: Zhang (2026) applies a Marxian framework to examine how AI and digital platform economies decouple labor input from value creation, arguing that traditional wage-setting mechanisms break down when algorithmic systems replace human cognitive work at scale. The paper calls for new theoretical extensions to account for AI-generated surplus and its distributional consequences. These findings bear directly on projections for median and entry-level wage trajectories.

highlights.title: Automation in Industry 4.0: Socio-Economic Trade-offs Beyond Efficiency Gains
highlights.summary: Qi (2026) investigates the socio-economic consequences of autonomous systems in industrial production, arguing that efficiency narratives obscure significant labor displacement and ethical risks as algorithmic autonomy replaces labor-intensive processes. The study stresses that workforce transition costs fall disproportionately on lower-skilled workers, exacerbating inequality. These findings are highly relevant to understanding displacement patterns in manufacturing and adjacent white-collar support roles.

highlights.title: Replacement vs. Augmentation: Romanian Academic Survey Maps AI Labor Market Perceptions
highlights.summary: Aivaz et al. (2026) survey Romanian students and faculty to assess whether AI is perceived primarily as a replacement or augmentation technology, finding significant divergence by discipline and seniority. Faculty in technical fields lean toward augmentation narratives while students in social sciences express higher displacement anxiety, suggesting AI literacy gaps shape risk perception. The results provide a leading-indicator lens on workforce AI exposure sentiment in an emerging European economy.

highlights.title: IoT, AI, and Robotics Strain Social Security Contributory Principles
highlights.summary: Cabeçais de Carvalho (2026) examines how the convergence of IoT, AI, cloud computing, and robotics disrupts the contributory basis of social security systems, as automation reduces the payroll tax base that funds pension and unemployment programs. The paper argues that current social protection architectures are structurally misaligned with an economy increasingly characterized by non-labor value creation. This has direct implications for the sustainability of safety nets during accelerated displacement.

themes: Structural displacement risk: Multiple papers converge on the view that AI-driven automation displaces workers faster than labor markets can reabsorb them, with competitive dynamics preventing voluntary firm-level restraint.
Wage theory under strain: Classical and Marxian wage models are being revisited as AI decouples labor input from value creation, threatening median and entry-level wage floors.

Perception gaps in AI exposure: Surveys reveal significant divergence in how workers and students perceive replacement vs. augmentation risk, with AI literacy strongly moderating displacement anxiety.

Social protection system vulnerability: The erosion of payroll-based contributory systems by automation is emerging as a macro-level policy risk, linking displacement directly to fiscal sustainability.

GenAI integration in education and software engineering: Multiple arxiv papers document rapid LLM adoption in higher education and software testing curricula, foreshadowing near-term shifts in entry-level tech and education labor demand.

watching.title: The Automation-Migration Interface and Migrants' Labour Market Integration
watching.reason: Explores how automation compounds integration barriers for migrant workers—an undertracked displacement channel with implications for entry-level wage and overall displacement graphs.

watching.title: LLMs for Software Testing Education: Experience Report
watching.reason: Documents LLM substitution for entry-level testing tasks in education; early signal for tech-sector displacement and entry-level wage compression if curriculum shifts accelerate.

watching.title: ManagerWorker: Can AI Models Direct Each Other?
watching.reason: Multi-agent AI pipelines that replace human task delegation hierarchies could accelerate white-collar and tech-sector displacement beyond single-task automation benchmarks.
